q: Use the bond dissociation energies in the table. What is ΔH for the overall reaction CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl + HCl, obtained by adding the two propagation steps?
h: Write the two propagation steps, find ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed) for each, and add them.
w: Step 1: Cl• + C–H → H–Cl + R•, ΔH = 413 − 431 = −18 kJ/mol. Step 2: R• + Cl–Cl → R–Cl + Cl•, ΔH = 242 − 354 = −112 kJ/mol. Sum = −130 kJ/mol. The same value comes from the net equation: broken C–H + Cl–Cl (655) minus formed H–Cl + C–Cl (785). Both chlorination steps are exothermic, which is why chlorination is fast and unselective.
x: −18 kJ/mol is only the first propagation step (H abstraction).
−112 kJ/mol is only the second propagation step (Cl transfer from Cl<sub>2</sub>).
Sign error: bonds formed (785) are stronger than bonds broken (655), so energy is released and ΔH is negative.

q: Methylenecyclohexane is treated with NBS and light. Which pair of constitutional isomers forms?
h: Find the allylic hydrogens, draw the allylic radical, and draw its resonance form. Each radical carbon can take Br.
w: The allylic H are on the ring CH2 groups next to C1 (C2 and C6 are equivalent). Removing one gives a radical delocalized between ring C2 and the exocyclic CH2: Br at C2 gives 1-bromo-2-methylidenecyclohexane; Br at the exocyclic carbon (allylic shift, C=C moves into the ring) gives 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexene. Those two products form; the shifted product has the more substituted (trisubstituted) alkene.
x: These are HBr-addition products (saturated). NBS substitutes an allylic H and keeps a C=C in the product.

3-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexene would need a radical at C3 of 1-methylcyclohexene, which is not formed from this starting alkene; the radical here is spread over ring C2 and the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon only.
A dibromide with the C=C gone is a Br<sub>2</sub>-addition product, which the low Br<sub>2</sub> concentration from NBS suppresses.

q: (E)-Pent-2-ene is treated with 1 equiv of NBS and light. Ignoring stereoisomers, what is the major product?
c: 4-Bromopent-2-ene (formed as a mixture of its stereoisomers)
1-Bromopent-2-ene, because the CH<sub>3</sub> group has more allylic H (3 vs 2)
h: There are two sets of allylic H. Which gives the more stable allylic radical, and are the two ends of that radical different?
w: Allylic H are on C1 (CH3, would give a 1° allylic radical) and C4 (CH2, gives a 2° allylic radical). Br• removes the C4 H because the radical is more stable. That radical, CH3–CH=CH–CH•–CH3 ↔ CH3–CH•–CH=CH–CH3, is symmetric: both ends are CH next to a CH3. Br at either end gives the same constitution, 4-bromopent-2-ene (as stereoisomers: a stereocenter and E/Z).
x: Statistics (3 H vs 2 H) are outweighed by radical stability; a 2° allylic C–H is clearly weaker than a 1° allylic C–H, and Br• is selective.
These two products come from the C1 (1° allylic) radical, which is the minor pathway.
A vicinal dibromide comes from Br<sub>2</sub> addition, which NBS suppresses by keeping Br<sub>2</sub> very low.

q: Radical polymerization of which monomer gives the polymer with repeat unit –[CH2–CH(CN)]n–?
h: In chain-growth polymerization the C=C becomes the backbone; every other atom of the monomer becomes a side group.
w: Each monomer adds through its C=C, which becomes two backbone carbons; substituents on those carbons become side groups. –[CH2–CH(CN)]– comes from CH2=CH–CN, acrylonitrile (polyacrylonitrile, used in acrylic fibers).
x: Propanenitrile has no C=C, so it cannot undergo chain-growth radical polymerization.
Methacrylonitrile would give –[CH<sub>2</sub>–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)(CN)]–, with an extra methyl on every other carbon.
A CN on both alkene carbons would give –[CH(CN)–CH(CN)]–, with a nitrile on every backbone carbon.

q: During radical polymerization of styrene, where does the growing chain radical add to a styrene molecule, and why?
c: To the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, because the new radical is benzylic and resonance-stabilized
To the CH carbon, because that carbon is less hindered
To the CH carbon, because the new radical is primary and more reactive toward the next monomer
To an aromatic ring carbon, because the ring has the most π electrons
h: Compare the two radicals you could make by adding to either end of the C=C.
w: Adding R• to the CH2 end leaves the odd electron on the carbon bearing the phenyl group, a benzylic radical delocalized into the ring. Adding to the CH end would give an unstabilized 1° radical. So addition occurs at CH2, giving the benzylic radical, and the chain grows head-to-tail with phenyl groups on alternating carbons.
x: The CH carbon carries the phenyl group, so it is the more hindered end, and attack there gives a poorly stabilized 1° radical.
Chain growth follows the more stable radical (lower E<sub>a</sub>), not the more reactive one; a 1° radical is formed much more slowly.
Adding to the ring would destroy aromaticity; the vinyl C=C is far more reactive toward radicals.

q: A small amount of a thiol (RSH) is added to the radical polymerization of styrene. The polymer still forms at nearly the same rate, but its average molar mass is much lower. What explains this?
c: A growing chain radical abstracts H from S–H, ending that chain, and RS• starts a new chain.
RSH combines with two growing chain radicals at once, stopping polymerization.
RSH adds across the C=C of styrene and turns monomer into an unreactive sulfide.
RSH breaks into H• and RS• on its own, adding more initiator and speeding up the reaction.
h: The number of radicals stays about the same, yet each chain is shorter. Which process ends one chain and immediately starts another?
w: This is chain transfer: P• + RS–H → P–H + RS•. The weak S–H bond gives up its H, so the growing chain stops, but the radical count is unchanged because RS• adds to styrene and starts a new chain. More, shorter chains form at about the same overall rate. Thiols are used as chain-transfer agents to control molar mass.
x: Removing radicals (termination) would slow the polymerization; the observation is that the rate hardly changes.
Converting monomer to an inert compound would lower yield, not specifically shorten each chain; the small amount of thiol works catalytically through its S–H bond.
Extra initiation would speed up the reaction; here the rate is nearly unchanged. RSH does not undergo homolysis on its own under these conditions.

q: Polyethylene made by high-pressure radical polymerization has many short branches (mostly butyl groups). Which process creates these branches?
c: The chain-end radical takes an H from five carbons back on its own chain, and the new mid-chain radical adds ethylene.
The chain-end radical adds to the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon of a butene impurity, which is then built into the growing chain.
Two chain-end radicals combine head-to-head, forming a branch point at the junction of the chains.
The chain-end radical rearranges by a 1,2-methyl shift to a more stable 2° radical, which keeps growing.
h: A primary chain-end radical can become a more stable 2° radical without adding monomer. Which kind of intramolecular step does that, and why would it favor a four-carbon branch?
w: This is intramolecular chain transfer ("backbiting"). The 1° chain-end radical reaches back through a six-membered cyclic transition state and abstracts an H from the CH2 five carbons away (a 1,5-H shift), giving a more stable 2° radical within the chain. Ethylene then adds at that site, so the four carbons past it become a butyl branch. Intermolecular H transfer between chains gives the long branches.
x: Butyl branches form in pure ethylene polymerization; they come from the chain itself, not from an impurity.
Combination of two radicals is termination: it joins two chains end-to-end into a linear chain, not a branched one.
A polyethylene chain end has no methyl group to shift, and 1,2-shifts are typical of carbocations, not radicals.

q: Di-tert-butyl peroxide is used as a radical initiator. Which bond breaks homolytically when it is heated?
h: Initiators contain one unusually weak bond.
w: The O–O bond of a peroxide is very weak (about 155 kJ/mol), far weaker than C–O, C–H or C–C bonds (about 350–420 kJ/mol). Heating breaks the O–O bond homolytically to give two (CH3)3CO• radicals, which start the chain.
x: C–O bonds are much stronger than the peroxide O–O bond, so they do not break at typical initiation temperatures.
C–H bonds are strong (about 400 kJ/mol or more); they are broken later by radicals in propagation, not in initiation.
C–C bonds are strong (about 350 kJ/mol); the initiator is designed with a much weaker bond elsewhere that breaks first.

q: Ethane is chlorinated with Cl2 and light. A trace of which product can form only by a termination step?
h: Which product needs two carbon radicals to meet each other?
w: Termination joins two radicals. Two ethyl radicals combine: 2 CH3CH2• → CH3CH2CH2CH3. Butane contains a new C–C bond that no propagation step can make, so traces of it are evidence for the radical chain mechanism. Chloroethane and HCl come from propagation; 1,1-dichloroethane comes from further propagation on chloroethane.
x: Chloroethane forms mainly in the propagation step CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl•.
1,1-Dichloroethane forms when chloroethane goes through the same propagation steps again (polychlorination).
HCl forms in every first propagation step, Cl• + C–H → H–Cl + C•.

q: Methylcyclohexane is monochlorinated with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light at 25 °C. Using relative rates per H of 1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 3.8 : 5, what percentage of the product is 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane?
h: Count every H as 1°, 2° or 3° (there are 14 H). Weight each class by its rate, then find the 3° share.
w: Methylcyclohexane has 3 primary H (CH3), 1 tertiary H (C1) and 10 secondary H (five ring CH2 groups). Weighted amounts: 1°: 3 × 1 = 3; 2°: 10 × 3.8 = 38; 3°: 1 × 5 = 5. Total = 46. 1-Chloro-1-methylcyclohexane = 5/46 = 11%. The many 2° H swamp the single more reactive 3° H.
x: 51% is 5/(1 + 3.8 + 5), which uses the rates but not the number of each kind of H.
7.1% is 1/14, the purely statistical share that ignores the higher reactivity of a 3° H.
33% (15.2/46) is the share of 1-chloro-2-methylcyclohexane (the four C2/C6 H), not of the 3° chloride.

q: Chlorination of propane with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light gives 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane in a 45 : 55 ratio. What is the reactivity of a secondary H relative to a primary H (per hydrogen)?
h: Divide each product amount by the number of hydrogens that lead to it, then take the ratio.
w: Propane has 6 primary H (giving 1-chloropropane) and 2 secondary H (giving 2-chloropropane). Per H: primary 45/6 = 7.5; secondary 55/2 = 27.5. Ratio 2° : 1° = 27.5/7.5 = 3.7.
x: 1.2 is 55/45, the product ratio without correcting for 6 primary vs 2 secondary H.
0.41 corrects the wrong way (55/45 × 2/6); the product from the fewer H must be divided by the smaller number.
7.3 divides only the primary amount by 6 and forgets to divide the secondary amount by 2.

q: Which sequence converts 2-methylbutane into 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product with the best selectivity?
c: 1. NBS, hν, CCl<sub>4</sub>  2. NaOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, heat
h: Step 1 must put the halogen on one specific carbon; step 2 must remove H to give the more substituted alkene.
w: Br2/hν is highly selective for the 3° C–H, giving mainly 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. A small, unhindered base (ethoxide) then performs Zaitsev E2 to give the trisubstituted alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene. Br2, hν, then NaOEt is the best route.
x: Cl<sub>2</sub> is unselective and gives a mixture of four monochlorides (only about 23% 3°), so many alkenes would form.
tert-Butoxide is bulky and gives mainly the Hofmann product, 2-methylbut-1-ene, from the 3° bromide.
NBS brominates allylic or benzylic positions; an alkane has no allylic H, so NBS is not the right reagent for this step.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Light means radicals. Which C–H bond in ethylbenzene gives the most stable radical?
w: Under radical conditions Br• removes the weakest C–H bond, the benzylic C–H (about 356 kJ/mol), giving a resonance-stabilized secondary benzylic radical. Br2 then delivers Br to that carbon: (1-bromoethyl)benzene, formed racemic because the planar radical reacts on both faces.
x: The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> gives a 1° radical that is not benzylic; that C–H bond is much stronger.
Ring bromination is electrophilic aromatic substitution and needs a Lewis acid such as FeBr<sub>3</sub>, not light.
Ortho ring bromination also requires FeBr<sub>3</sub> (electrophilic substitution); hν leads to radical substitution at the benzylic carbon.

q: cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane (a meso compound) is treated with Br2 and light. Which statement best describes the 1-bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane formed?
c: Two diastereomers (Br cis or trans to the C2 methyl), each formed as a racemic mixture
One meso compound, because the starting alkane is meso
Two diastereomers, each formed as a single enantiomer, because C2 keeps its configuration
One diastereomer, as a racemic mixture, because Br always adds trans to the C2 methyl
h: Which H is removed? Look at the two tertiary H: how are they related in a meso compound? Then ask what the planar radical can do.
w: Br• removes a 3° H (on C1 or C2). In the meso alkane those two H are enantiotopic, so they react at the same rate, giving enantiomeric radicals in equal amounts. Each planar radical takes Br from either face, so Br ends up cis or trans to the remaining methyl-bearing stereocenter: two diastereomers, and because the two radicals are mirror images, each diastereomer forms as a 1:1 pair of enantiomers. Answer: two diastereomers, each racemic. (The product is chiral; it has no internal mirror plane.)
x: 1-Bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane has two different stereocenters (C1 bears Br, C2 bears H), so no stereoisomer of it is meso.
C2 keeps its configuration within one radical, but the H at C1 and the H at C2 are mirror-image (enantiotopic) and react equally, so every product forms together with its enantiomer.
Neither face of the radical is fully blocked; both diastereomers form, though not necessarily in equal amounts.

q: Radical iodination of alkanes (I<sub>2</sub>, hν) does not occur to a useful extent. Given BDEs of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–H = 413, H–I = 297, I–I = 151 and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–I = 234 kJ/mol, what is the main reason?
c: H abstraction by I• is endothermic by about 116 kJ/mol, too slow to sustain a chain.
The I–I bond is too strong to be broken by light, so no I• forms to start the chain.
Transfer of I from I<sub>2</sub> to the alkyl radical is endothermic by about 83 kJ/mol.
I• is so reactive that it abstracts every kind of H equally and gives only product mixtures.
h: Calculate ΔH for each propagation step. Which one is the problem?
w: Step 1: I• + R–H → H–I + R•, ΔH = 413 − 297 = +116 kJ/mol, steeply uphill, so Ea is at least 116 kJ/mol and the step is far too slow for a chain. Step 2: R• + I–I → R–I + I•, ΔH = 151 − 234 = −83 kJ/mol, which is fine. The endothermic H-abstraction step stops iodination.
x: I–I (151 kJ/mol) is the weakest of the halogen–halogen bonds, so visible light splits it easily; initiation is not the problem.
Sign error: ΔH = 151 − 234 = −83 kJ/mol; the iodine-transfer step is exothermic.
I• is the least reactive halogen atom; the problem is too little reactivity, not too much.
